{{Short description|Family of modal logics for agency and choice}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2025}}
{{AI-generated|reason=see the explanation at [[Special:PermanentLink/1368212033#Query]]|date=August 2026}}

'''STIT logic''' (from ''seeing to it that'') is a family of [[modal logic|modal]] and [[temporal logic|branching-time]] logics for reasoning about agency and choice. A typical STIT operator has the form <math>[i\ \mathsf{stit}:\varphi]</math>, usually read as "agent <math>i</math> sees to it that <math>\varphi</math>", and is interpreted in models where agents choose between alternative possible futures.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001>{{cite book |last=Belnap |first=Nuel |author2=Perloff, Michael |author3=Xu, Ming |year=2001 |title=Facing the Future: Agents and Choices in Our Indeterminist World |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |doi=10.1093/oso/9780195138788.001.0001 |isbn=978-0-19-513878-8 }}</ref><ref name=TemporalSEP>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Goranko |first=Valentin |year=2015 |title=Temporal Logic |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-temporal/}}</ref>

STIT logics are used in [[action theory (philosophy)|action theory]], [[deontic logic]], [[epistemic logic]], and the theory of [[intelligent agent]]s to formalise notions such as "could have done otherwise", responsibility, joint action, and strategic ability in an indeterministic world.<ref name=Segerberg1992>{{cite journal |last=Segerberg |first=Krister |year=1992 |title=Getting started: Beginnings in the logic of action |journal=Studia Logica |volume=51 |issue=3–4 |pages=347–378 |doi=10.1007/BF01028968}}</ref><ref name=Horty2001>{{cite book |last=Horty |first=John F. |year=2001 |title=Agency and Deontic Logic |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The acronym '''STIT''' comes from the English phrase "seeing to it that", introduced in influential work by Nuel Belnap and Michael Perloff on the logical analysis of agentive expressions.<ref name=BelnapPerloff1988>{{cite journal |last=Belnap |first=Nuel |author2=Perloff, Michael |year=1988 |title=Seeing to it that: A canonical form for agentives |journal=Theoria |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=175–199 |doi=10.1111/j.1755-2567.1988.tb00700.x |doi-broken-date=29 January 2026 }}</ref> In this tradition, "to see to it that <math>\varphi</math>" is treated as a primitive agency operator, rather than being reduced to ordinary modal necessity.

==History==
Modern STIT logic arose in the 1980s in the context of branching-time semantics and formal theories of agency. Belnap and Perloff's article "Seeing to it that: A canonical form for agentives" introduced the idea of treating expressions of the form "agent ''i'' sees to it that φ" as a primitive modal operator, and analysed such sentences using a branching tree of moments and histories.<ref name=BelnapPerloff1988 /> This approach was further developed in a series of papers on indeterminism and agency and provided the conceptual core for later STIT formalisms.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /><ref name=Muller2014>{{cite book |last=Müller |first=Thomas |year=2014 |chapter=Introduction: The many branches of Belnap's logic |title=Nuel Belnap on Indeterminism and Free Action |editor=Thomas Müller |series=Outstanding Contributions to Logic |volume=2 |publisher=Springer |location=Cham |pages=1–34 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-01754-9_1 |isbn=978-3-319-01753-2 }}</ref>

In the 1990s the basic formal systems of STIT logic were worked out. Horty and Belnap's influential paper on the deliberative STIT operator distinguished between a "[[Brian Chellas|Chellas]]" STIT that merely records the result of an agent's present choice and a "deliberative" STIT that requires the agent's choice to make a difference, and connected STIT with issues of action, omission, ability and obligation.<ref name=HortyBelnap1995>{{cite journal |last1=Horty |first1=John F. |last2=Belnap |first2=Nuel |year=1995 |title=The deliberative stit: A study of action, omission, ability, and obligation |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=24 |issue=6 |pages=583–644 |doi=10.1007/BF01306968}}</ref> Around the same time, Ming Xu proved completeness and decidability results for basic STIT systems, including a single-agent logic with Kripke-style semantics and axiomatizations for multi-agent deliberative STIT, thereby establishing STIT as a well-behaved normal modal framework.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Xu |first=Ming |year=1995 |title=On the basic logic of STIT with a single agent |journal=Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=60 |issue=2 |pages=459–483 |doi=10.2307/2275620 |jstor=2275620 }}</ref><ref name=Xu1998 />

This early work was systematised in Belnap, Perloff and Xu's monograph ''Facing the Future: Agents and Choices in Our Indeterminist World'', which presents a general branching-time semantics for individual and group STIT operators, discusses independence-of-agents conditions and articulates the metaphysical picture of an indeterministic "tree" of moments.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /><ref name=Muller2014 /> At roughly the same time, Horty's book ''Agency and Deontic Logic'' developed deontic STIT logics in which obligations are tied to agents' available choices rather than to static states of affairs, and used the resulting systems to analyse "ought implies can", contrary-to-duty obligations and deontic paradoxes.<ref name=Horty2001 /><ref name=McNamara2004 /> These works helped to position STIT at the intersection of [[Action theory (philosophy)|action theory]], [[temporal logic]] and [[deontic logic]].

From the late 1990s and 2000s onward, STIT logics were combined with epistemic, temporal and strategic modalities. Broersen introduced complete STIT logics for knowledge and action and deontic-epistemic STIT systems that distinguish different modes of ''mens rea'', with applications to responsibility and the specification of multi-agent systems.<ref name=Broersen2009 /><ref>{{cite journal |last=Broersen |first=Jan M. |year=2011 |title=Deontic epistemic stit logic distinguishing modes of mens rea |journal=Journal of Applied Logic |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=137–152 |doi=10.1016/j.jal.2010.06.002}}</ref> Work on group and coalitional agency investigated axiomatisations and complexity results for group STIT logics,<ref name=BalbianiHerzigTroquard2008>{{cite journal |last1=Balbiani |first1=Philippe |last2=Herzig |first2=Andreas |last3=Troquard |first3=Nicolas |year=2008 |title=Alternative axiomatics and complexity of deliberative STIT theories |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=387–406 |doi=10.1007/s10992-007-9078-7 |arxiv=0704.3238 }}</ref> and related STIT-based analyses of agency to coalition logic and alternating-time temporal logic (ATL) by exhibiting formal embeddings between the frameworks.<ref name="Pauly 2001 135–165">{{cite journal |last=Pauly |first=Marc |year=2001 |title=Logic for social software |journal=Journal of Applied Non-Classical Logics |volume=11 |issue=1–2 |pages=135–165}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alur |first1=Rajeev |last2=Henzinger |first2=Thomas A. |last3=Kupferman |first3=Orna |year=2002 |title=Alternating-time temporal logic |journal=Journal of the ACM |volume=49 |issue=5 |pages=672–713 |doi=10.1145/585265.585270}}</ref><ref name="Broersen 2006 559–578">{{cite journal |last=Broersen |first=Jan M. |year=2006 |title=Embedding Alternating-time Temporal Logic in strategic STIT logic of agency |journal=Journal of Logic and Computation |volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=559–578 |doi=10.1093/logcom/exl006}}</ref>

Explicit temporal operators were added to STIT in so-called temporal STIT logics. Lorini proposed a temporal STIT with "next" and "until" operators along histories and showed how it can be applied to normative reasoning about ongoing behaviour and commitments.<ref name=Lorini2013>{{cite journal |last=Lorini |first=Emiliano |year=2013 |title=Temporal STIT logic and its application to normative reasoning |journal=Journal of Applied Non-Classical Logics |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=372–399 |doi=10.1080/11663081.2013.861302 |doi-broken-date=29 January 2026 }}</ref> Ciuni and Lorini compared different semantics for temporal STIT, clarifying the relationships between branching-time, game-based and epistemic approaches,<ref name=CiuniLorini2018>{{cite journal |last1=Ciuni |first1=Roberto |last2=Lorini |first2=Emiliano |year=2018 |title=Comparing semantics for temporal STIT logic |journal=Logique et Analyse |series=New Series |volume=61 |issue=243 |pages=299–339}}</ref> while Boudou and Lorini gave a semantics for temporal STIT based on concurrent game structures, thus strengthening links with standard models of multi-agent interaction used for ATL and strategy logic.<ref name=BoudouLorini2018>{{cite conference |last1=Boudou |first1=Joseph dangerously undecidable |title=Proceedings of the 21st European Conference on Artificial Intelligence (ECAI 2014) |pages=1093–1094}}</ref>

In the 2010s, STIT ideas were combined with justification logic, imagination operators and refined deontic notions. Justification STIT logics, developed by Olkhovikov and others, merge explicit justifications with STIT-style agency so that producing a proof can itself be treated as an action that brings about knowledge, and they come with completeness and decidability results.<ref name=Olkhovikov2019Just>{{cite journal |last=Olkhovikov |first=Grigory K. |year=2019 |title=The basics of justification STIT logic |journal=Studia Logica |volume=107 |issue=4 |pages=713–742 |doi=10.1007/s11225-017-9779-z}}</ref> Olkhovikov and Wansing introduced STIT imagination logics, together with axiomatic systems and tableau calculi, to model acts of voluntary imagining and their role in doxastic control.<ref name=OlkhovikovWansing2018>{{cite journal |last1=Olkhovikov |first1=Grigory K. |last2=Wansing imagination logic |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=48 |issue=6 |pages=981–1001 |doi=10.1007/s10992-019-09503-1}}</ref> Other authors have proposed STIT-based logics of responsibility, blameworthiness and intentionality for use in philosophical and AI settings.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Baltag |first1=Alexandru |last2=Canavotto |first2=Ilaria |last3=Smets |first3=Sonja |year=2020 Current research on STIT focuses on proof theory, automated reasoning and richer expressive resources. Lyon and van Berkel, building on earlier work on labelled calculi for STIT, have developed cut-free sequent systems and proof-search algorithms that yield syntactic decision procedures for a range of deontic and non-deontic multi-agent STIT logics and support applications such as duty checking and compliance checking in autonomous systems.<ref name=LyonBerkel2024>{{cite journal |last1=Lyon ==Branching-time semantics==
STIT logics are usually interpreted over [[branching time|branching-time]] models. A standard STIT frame consists of:<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /><ref name=TemporalSEP />
* a non-empty set of '''moments''' <math>T</math>, partially ordered by <math><</math> so that <math>(T,<)</math> forms a tree (every pair of moments with a common predecessor has a greatest lower bound);
* a set of '''histories''', each history being a maximal linearly ordered subset of <math>T</math>;
* a non-empty set of agents <math>Ag</math>;
* for each agent <math>i \in Ag</math> and moment <math>m</math>, a '''choice function''' <math>\mathsf{choice}_i^m</math> that partitions the set of histories passing through <math>m</math> into '''choice cells'''.

The idea is that a moment represents a time at which choices are made, and histories represent complete possible future courses of events. At each moment, each agent's choice corresponds to selecting one of the available cells of histories determined by their choice function.

Formulas are evaluated at pairs <math>(m,h)</math> of a moment and a history through that moment (sometimes written <math>m/h</math>). A valuation assigns truth-values to atomic propositions at such indices; Boolean connectives are interpreted pointwise as in [[Kripke semantics|Kripke-style]] modal logic.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 />

==Chellas and deliberative STIT operators==
Several STIT operators have been distinguished in the literature. A common approach uses two closely related operators, often called '''Chellas STIT''' and '''deliberative STIT'''.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /><ref name=Xu1998>{{cite journal |last=Xu |first=Ming |year=1998 |title=Axioms for deliberative STIT |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=27 |issue=5 |pages=505–552 |doi=10.1023/A:1004288801405 |doi-broken-date=29 January 2026 }}</ref>

Let <math>H_m</math> be the set of histories passing through a moment <math>m</math>, and write <math>H_m</math> <math>\text{⟦}\varphi\text{⟧}_m = \{ h \in H_m \mid M,m/h \models \varphi \}</math> for the set of histories at <math>m</math> where <math>\varphi</math> holds.

* The '''Chellas STIT''' operator, often written <math>[i\ \mathsf{cstit}:\varphi]</math>, is given by
::<math>M,m/h \models [i\ \mathsf{cstit}:\varphi] \quad\text{iff}\quad \mathsf{choice}_i^m(h) \subseteq \text{⟦}\varphi\text{⟧}_m.</math>
::Intuitively, agent <math>i</math> sees to it that <math>\varphi</math> if <math>\varphi</math> holds at all histories compatible with their present choice.

* The '''deliberative STIT''' operator, <math>[i\ \mathsf{dstit}:\varphi]</math>, adds a "non-triviality" or "negative" condition:
::<math>M,m/h \models [i\ \mathsf{dstit}:\varphi]</math> iff <math>M,m/h \models [i\ \mathsf{cstit}:\varphi]</math> and <math>\varphi</math> is not already historically necessary at <math>m</math> (i.e. fails at some history through <math>m</math>).<ref name=Xu1998 />

To express the latter, a '''historic necessity''' operator <math>\Box_H</math> is often defined by
::<math>M,m/h \models \Box_H \varphi \quad\text{iff}\quad \text{for all } h' \in H_m,\, M,m/h' \models \varphi.</math>

On this basis, Chellas and deliberative STIT become interdefinable by:
::<math>[i\ \mathsf{dstit}:\varphi] \leftrightarrow \bigl([i\ \mathsf{cstit}:\varphi] \land \neg \Box_H \varphi\bigr),</math>
::<math>[i\ \mathsf{cstit}:\varphi] \leftrightarrow \bigl([i\ \mathsf{dstit}:\varphi] \lor \Box_H \varphi\bigr).</math><ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 />

Ming Xu proved completeness results and axiomatizations for basic dstit logics with single and multiple agents, establishing STIT as a well-behaved modal system.<ref name=Xu1998 /><ref name=TemporalSEP />

==Group agency and joint action==
STIT models naturally support notions of group and collective agency. Given a set of agents <math>G \subseteq Ag</math>, a group STIT operator <math>[G\ \mathsf{stit}:\varphi]</math> can be defined so that it is true exactly when the collective choices of all agents in <math>G</math> guarantee <math>\varphi</math>.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /> Different notions of joint agency (for instance, where all group members are essential vs. inessential participants) can be distinguished by constraints on the choice functions for groups and individuals.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /><ref>{{cite journal |last=Zanardo |first=Alberto |year=2013 |title=Indistinguishability, choices, and logics of agency |journal=Studia Logica |volume=101 |issue=2 |pages=287–310 |doi=10.1007/s11225-013-9530-3}}</ref>

Group STIT operators have been combined with temporal and epistemic operators to study collective responsibilities, joint intentions, and coordination in [[multi-agent system]]s.<ref name=Broersen2009>{{cite book |last=Broersen |first=Jan M. |year=2009 |chapter=A complete STIT logic for knowledge and action, and some of its applications |editor=Matteo Baldoni |editor2=Tran Cao Son |editor3=M. Birna van Riemsdijk |editor4=Michael Winikoff |title=Declarative Agent Languages and Technologies VI |publisher=Springer |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=5422 |pages=47–59 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-03839-8_3 |doi-broken-date=29 January 2026 }}</ref>

==Deontic and normative STIT==
STIT logic has been combined with [[deontic logic]] to model obligations and permissions that concern an agent's actions rather than mere states of affairs. John F. Horty developed a deontic STIT framework in which obligations to act are evaluated against an indeterministic branching-time background, allowing for a distinction between "ought-to-do" and "ought-to-be" and addressing classic deontic paradoxes.<ref name=Horty2001 /><ref name=McNamara2004>{{cite journal |last=McNamara |first=Paul |year=2004 |title=Review of John F. Horty, ''Agency and Deontic Logic'' |journal=Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews |url=https://ndpr.nd.edu/reviews/agency-and-deontic-logic/}}</ref> See {{section link|Agentive logic|John Horty's ought-to-do logic}}.

Subsequent work has explored deontic STIT logics for formalising contrary-to-duty obligations, prioritised norms, and policies in computational normative systems, and for connecting STIT-based notions of agency with [[input/output logic]] and other frameworks for normative reasoning.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gabbay |first=Dov |author2=Horty, John F. |author3=Parent, Xavier |author4=van der Torre, Leendert |author5=others |year=2013 |title=Handbook of Deontic Logic and Normative Systems |publisher=College Publications |location=London}}</ref><ref name="Olkhovikov2019Just"/>

==Temporal and epistemic extensions==
Although the original STIT systems used an implicit branching-time background, later work has combined STIT with explicit temporal operators, resulting in '''temporal STIT''' logics. These add connectives for "next", "always", or "until" along histories, allowing reasoning about what agents can ensure over time.<ref name=TemporalSEP /><ref name="Lorini2013"/>

Epistemic and doxastic STIT logics enrich the framework with operators for knowledge and belief, enabling analysis of "knowingly doing", informational responsibility, and strategic ignorance.<ref name=Broersen2009 /> Justification STIT logics merge STIT with [[justification logic]], modelling proofs or justifications as actions that result in knowledge.<ref name="Olkhovikov2019Just"/>

==Relationships to other logics==
STIT logic is closely related to, but distinct from, several other modal frameworks:

* Like [[branching time|branching-time temporal logic]], it uses tree-like models with histories, but STIT operators focus on agents' choices rather than temporal quantification alone.<ref name=TemporalSEP /><ref name=BranchingTimeSEP>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Spolaore |first=Giuliano |year=2025 |title=Branching Time |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/branching-time/}}</ref>
* Compared to [[dynamic logic (modal logic)|dynamic logic]], which treats actions as program-like relations between states, STIT treats actions implicitly via partitions of histories determined by agents' choices; some authors have studied embeddings and combinations of these perspectives.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /><ref>{{cite book |last=Broersen |first=Jan M. |year=2009 |chapter=Combinations of STIT and actions |editor=Hinrichs |title=Essays in Logic and Practical Reasoning |publisher=Springer}}</ref>
* [[Coalition logic]] and [[alternating-time temporal logic]] (ATL) analyse what groups of agents can achieve by choosing strategies; STIT's group operators are closely related and there are formal embeddings in both directions.<ref name="Pauly 2001 135–165"/><ref>{{cite journal |last=Alur |first=Rajeev |author2=Henzinger, Thomas A. |author3=Kupferman, Orna |year=2002 |title=Alternating-time temporal logic |journal=Journal of the ACM |volume=49 |issue=5 |pages=672–713 |doi=10.1145/585265.585270}}</ref><ref name="Broersen 2006 559–578"/>

==Applications==
===Philosophy===
In [[philosophy of action]] and [[metaphysics]], STIT logics model free will, alternative possibilities, and moral responsibility in indeterministic settings. The framework has been used to articulate conditions under which agents "could have done otherwise", and to analyse the compatibility of free agency with branching-time metaphysics.<ref name=BelnapEtAl2001 /><ref name=Muller2014 />

In [[ethics]] and [[deontic logic]], deontic STIT connects obligations with agents' available choices and abilities, providing tools to reason about "ought implies can", contrary-to-duty obligations, and practical dilemmas.<ref name=Horty2001 /><ref name=McNamara2004 /> [[Agentive logic#John Horty's ought-to-do logic|John Horty's ought-to-do logic]], created for modelling agentive duties, was developed based on STIT operators.

===Computer science and artificial intelligence===
In [[computer science]] and [[artificial intelligence]], STIT-based logics contribute to the specification and verification of [[multi-agent system]]s, autonomous agents, and normative systems. Temporal-epistemic STIT logics have been proposed as specification languages for agents with knowledge, goals, and actions, and have been related to more mainstream modal logics used in [[model checking]].<ref name=Broersen2009 /><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Thomason |first=Richmond H. |year=2018 |title=Logic and Artificial Intelligence |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/}}</ref>

STIT ideas have also been combined with justification and proof-theoretic formalisms to represent reasoning as an activity that produces knowledge, and to study interactions between agency and proof in formal systems.<ref name="Olkhovikov2019Just"/>
